items.text: There is an explicit formula for how each cell’s area changes under a small move. I checked it against recomputed diagrams, and it gives an analytic direction for reducing the mean weight difference when the objective is smooth. Finding the best final position still requires more than that local calculation.

There is a more concrete result: **for the mean absolute weight difference, we can calculate the steepest local improvement direction explicitly from the current diagram.** This gives an analytic rule for moving the center, although it does not directly give the globally optimal destination.

Keep every other center fixed. Call the moving center \(p\), with density \(\rho_i\). For each neighboring center \(q_j\), let:

- \(\ell_j\) be the length of their shared edge.
- \(m_j\) be the midpoint of that edge.
- \(d_j=\|q_j-p\|\) be the distance between the centers.

Define the vector
\[
b_j=\frac{\ell_j}{d_j}(m_j-p),
\qquad
B=\sum_j b_j.
\]

**These vectors tell us exactly how areas respond to an infinitesimal move.** For a small displacement \(h\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{change in your cell’s area}
   &=B\cdot h+o(\|h\|),\\
\text{change in neighbor }j\text{’s area}
   &=-b_j\cdot h+o(\|h\|).
\end{aligned}
\]
The area gained across a shared edge is precisely the area lost by the neighbor. These are the planar forms of standard Voronoi volume derivatives. [Kincl et al., Theorem 1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/fld.5339)

Now let
\[
D_j=W_i-W_j
\]
be the current weight difference. Since each center keeps its density, the derivative of this difference with respect to \(p\) is
\[
\nabla_pD_j=\rho_i B+\rho_j b_j.
\]

Consequently, for your objective
\[
F(p)=\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}|W_i(p)-W_j(p)|,
\]
we obtain the explicit formula
\[
\boxed{
\nabla_pF
=\frac1k\sum_{j=1}^{k}
\operatorname{sign}(W_i-W_j)
\bigl(\rho_iB+\rho_jb_j\bigr).
}
\]

The gradient is a two-dimensional vector. **Moving in its opposite direction decreases the average discrepancy**, provided the gradient is nonzero, the move is sufficiently small and feasible, and we are away from weight equalities or changes in adjacency.

That gives a practical procedure:

1. Calculate the current cells, weights, and shared edges.
2. Calculate the vector above.
3. Take a step in the opposite direction, shortening it until the recomputed diagram actually improves the objective.
4. Repeat.

The step size and final destination still require numerical work. Weight equalities need nonsmooth optimization, and a local optimum need not be globally best.

For the **median** objective, another distinction becomes clear: with an odd number of neighbors and no ties in the ordered absolute differences, its local derivative depends only on the neighbor occupying the middle rank. With an even number, the usual median depends on the middle two. Thus the median can locally ignore even very large discrepancies, whereas the mean includes every neighbor.

items.text:
**It has an exact mathematical formulation and analytic derivatives, but in general you should expect to find the optimal location numerically, rather than through a simple closed-form formula.**

Since each center keeps its density, let \(\rho_j\) denote center \(j\)’s weight per unit area. Move center \(i\) to a candidate position \(p\), keep the other centers fixed, and recompute the diagram. Each cell’s weight is then
\[
W_j(p)=\rho_j\,\operatorname{Area}(V_j(p)).
\]

Let \(N_i(p)\) be the centers whose cells share an edge with cell \(i\). Interpreting “difference” as **absolute difference**, your two proposed objectives are
\[
F_{\mathrm{mean}}(p)
=\frac{1}{|N_i(p)|}
\sum_{j\in N_i(p)}|W_i(p)-W_j(p)|
\]
and
\[
F_{\mathrm{median}}(p)
=\operatorname{median}_{j\in N_i(p)}
|W_i(p)-W_j(p)|.
\]
The task is to minimize the chosen function over allowed positions \(p\).

The difficulty is that **moving one center changes both its own cell and its neighbors’ cells**. Although the boundaries are straight, their positions and intersections depend nonlinearly on \(p\).

For a fixed pattern of edges and vertices, the cell areas can be expressed as rational functions of the two coordinates of \(p\). Thus, one can derive formulas and derivatives within each such configuration. But finding the global minimum requires accounting for changes in that configuration, absolute-value corners, and—for the median—changes in the ordering of the differences. A local minimum need not be the global minimum.

Two modeling details matter:

- **Original or resulting neighbors?** Your wording could mean either. Using the resulting neighbors can make the objective jump when a neighbor appears or disappears. Fixing the original neighbor list avoids that particular issue.
- **Mean or median?** The median can be small while some neighbors remain very different. Mean absolute difference is a more direct measure of balancing against all neighbors.

Perfect equality may also be impossible when only one center can move.

The broader problem is related to **equitable partitioning**, for which analytical results and iterative algorithms exist, including approaches using power diagrams. Those approaches allow different adjustments from your single-center move. [Pavone et al., *Distributed Algorithms for Environment Partitioning*](https://web.stanford.edu/~pavone/papers/Pavone.Arsie.ea.TAC11.pdf)
Understood. If I need clarification, I’ll ask an open-ended question without preset choices.

Let \(P\) be a polygonal region in the plane, and let \(S=\{c_1,\ldots,c_n\}\) be a finite set of distinct centers inside \(P\).

The **bounded Voronoi diagram** of \(S\) in \(P\) is the collection of cells
\[
V_i=\{x\in P:\|x-c_i\|\le \|x-c_j\|\text{ for every }j\}.
\]

Thus, each cell contains all points in \(P\) for which its center is a closest center. The cells cover \(P\), and ties belong to the shared boundaries of the corresponding cells.

If \(P\) is convex, every cell is a convex polygon.

content.text: does a bounded Voronoi diagram consist only of straight lines?

items.text:
Yes—using ordinary Euclidean distance and a polygonal enclosing boundary, every cell boundary consists of **straight line segments**.

Each segment lies either on the perpendicular bisector between two centers or on an edge of the enclosing polygon.

content.text: good.what is the name of this structure? does it have a name?

items.text:
It’s called a **Voronoi diagram clipped to a polygon**, or a **bounded Voronoi diagram**.

The region assigned to each center is its **Voronoi cell**; the centers are often called **sites**.

content.text: ok, so given a polygon and a set of centers inside it, the boundaries of each such center form a polygon right?

items.text:
**Yes, if the enclosing polygon is convex.** Each center’s region is the intersection of its Voronoi cell with the enclosing polygon, so it is also a convex polygon. Its boundary includes both the closest-center contours and any relevant parts of the enclosing polygon’s boundary.

If the enclosing polygon is **nonconvex**, a center’s region still has straight edges, but it can be disconnected—so it need not be a single polygon.

content.text: assume a finite set of dots on the plane call them centers, and for each center, assign every dot in the place to its closest center if there is one.  a contour dot is a dot with equal distance to two centers.  question: do the contour dots form polygons?

items.text:
You’re describing a **Voronoi diagram**, with one important clarification: a contour point should be equally distant from **two or more closest centers**. Being equally distant from two centers doesn’t make it a boundary if another center is closer.

**The boundaries form straight-edged regions, but not all of those regions are closed polygons.** Some extend to infinity.

To see why, let \(a\) and \(b\) be two centers. The points closer to \(a\) than to \(b\) lie on \(a\)’s side of the perpendicular bisector of the segment \(ab\). Thus the region belonging to \(a\) is
\[
V_a=\bigcap_{b\ne a}\{x:\|x-a\|\le \|x-b\|\}.
\]
Each set in this intersection is a half-plane. Since there are finitely many centers, their intersection is a convex region bounded by straight edges.

So:

- Every **bounded** region is a convex polygon.
- **Unbounded** regions can have edges that are infinite rays or entire lines.
- With just two centers, the entire contour is one straight line—not a polygon.

If you restrict the diagram to a rectangle, all the resulting regions are convex polygons, with parts of the rectangle’s boundary completing their outlines.
